Assertive sentence or Statement — is a sentence which gives us information about something. It can be in the affirmative or it can be Negative.
Science is an interesting subject. — Affirmative I did not meet my friends yesterday — Negative
Interrogative sentence or Question — is a sentence which raises a question to get some information about something. It ends with a question mark. It can also be in the affirmative or negative.
Do you study your lessons daily?
— Affirmative Didn’t they pay their taxes on time?
— Negative Is your father buying a new car?
— Affirmative Aren’t you selling the old house?
— Negative Why doesn’t your brother come in time?
— Negative When did you come to India?
Imperative sentence — is a sentence which gives orders, makes requests or gives advice. It ends with a full stop. It may be affirmative and negative.
Bring me a glass of water (Order)
Exclamatory sentence — is a sentence that expresses some strong or sudden feeling.
What a beauty! How happily they are living!
Optative sentence — is a sentence that expresses a wish, probability or supposition.
May God help you. I wish they would be with me.
In a sentence words are labeled according to their function, it is called parts of speech. They are eight in number, Noun, Pronoun, Adjective, Verb, Adverb, Preposition, Conjunction and Interjection.
A word which tells the name of a person, place or a thing is called a noun.
There are five kinds of nouns:
Proper Noun: Names of specific person, place or a thing is known as a proper noun.
Common Noun: Names given in common to every person or thing of the same class or kind.
Collective Noun: Collection of persons or things taken together and spoken as a whole.
Army, flock, class, team, fleet, jury, family, nation, committee.
Material Noun: a noun that stands for matter or substance.
Abstract Noun: Denoting a thing which we cannot see or touch.
Truth, hope, honesty, health, courage, pain, joy, sleep, death, Bravery, sickness.

Any noun that stands for only one person or thing is said to be in Singular number. Any noun that stands for more than one person or things is said to be in Plural number.
Note: Uncountable nouns are rarely used in plural. Gold, Dust, Smoke, Furniture, Dirt, Sugar and Milk – never to be used in plural forms — always singular.
The following nouns have the same form for the singular as well as plural. Sheep: There is a sheep in the field. These sheep have no wool on them.
I bought a dozen of mangoes.
She gave us five dozen apples.
The fish is swimming in the pond.
He gave me a score of pencils.
He lived for four score years.
The following nouns are always used in singular: Furniture, news, scenery, innings, mathematics, physics.
The following nouns are always used in plural: Alms, Cattle, People, Scissors, Trousers, Spectacles, Riches, Clothes, Poultry, Vermal, Gentry.
He did many acts of mischief.
He gave us many pieces of advice.
His house is built of stones.
His house is built of stone.
He had a bag of rices.
He had a bag of rice.
He was fond of bad companies.
He was fond of bad company.

We should always say: The members of his family have come. There is no room in this compartment. Always help the poor, the needy. The blotting paper is mine. We had a good game of hockey. He gave me a ten-rupee note. He is a five year old child. There is a three foot rule. We have purchased a piece of ground on Salai road.
Fish and hair – Singular when they are used collectively, otherwise always plural.
There is a plenty of fish here. There were some red and white fishes caught. Mary has a golden hair. He has few white hairs in his beard.

My scissors (is, are) not very sharp. Mathematics (is, are) a difficult subject. The hunter shot there (deer, deers). The (scenery, sceneries) of the Himalayas is very fine. The room is full of (furnitures, furniture). Her (hair, hairs) (is, are) brown. The (cattle, cattles) are grazing in the field. (Alm, Alms) (were, was) given to the (poor, Poors). Fifty (Sheep, sheeps) are grazing in the field. He gave her five (hundred, Hundreds).
A pronoun is a word used instead of a noun.
John is absent, he is ill.

Demonstrative Pronoun: this, that, these, those, and such. Distributive Pronoun: each, either, neither. Indefinite Pronoun: all, some, many, few, none, and such other. Relative Pronoun: who, which, whose, whom. Reflexive Pronoun: Myself, yourself, himself, herself. (They are also called Emphasizing Pronouns.)

This is a man. He stole my purse. → This is a man who stole my purse. This is a boy. His nature is good. → This is a boy whose nature is good. This is a pen. Jim likes it most. → This is a pen which Jim likes most. This is a house. Jack built it. → This is a house that Jack built. This is a boy. The teacher praised him. → This is a boy whom the teacher praised.
An adjective is a word used to add to the meaning of a noun.
He is an intelligent boy. Akbar was a brave king.
There are six kinds of adjectives.
Adjectives of Quantity — it answers the question “How much?”
He had much money. There is little food in the house. He wants some money. He did not eat any bread. He had sufficient bread. He ate the whole cake.
Adjective of Number — answering the question, “How many?”
All men are mortal. Many women were not there. Several men came to see the line. He had five rupees in his pocket. Some men are rich. The first boy won the prize. Most men are lazy.
